title: Reading and Writing Text Files
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of reading and writing text files and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.

content.intro: Reading and Writing Text Files is part of Working with Files, Directories, and External Data. Start with readlines() and writelines() and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Text processing should distinguish matching values from near-misses and account for missing text and encoding.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Text processing should distinguish matching values from near-misses and account for missing text and encoding. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: Check matching and non-matching text, whitespace, missing strings and encoding assumptions. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For reading and writing text files, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
